label: thm:contraction
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:contraction}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=0pt,topsep=1pt,label=(\alph*)]
\item For every $H\in\mathcal{B}_n$, $\sigma_2(H)\le 1-n\,\delta(H)$. Equality holds for $H=(1-t)P_\pi+tJ/n$, $t\in[0,1]$.
\item For $l<L$, $\sigma_2(H_{L:l})\le\prod_{i=l}^{L-1}\sigma_2(H_i)\le\exp\big(-n\sum_{i=l}^{L-1}\delta(H_i)\big)$.
\item $\max_{jk}\big|(H_{L:l})_{jk}-\tfrac1n\big|\le\sigma_2(H_{L:l})$. Thus $H_{L:l}\to J/n$ entrywise if $\sum_i\delta(H_i)\to\infty$.
\item Let $H=\mathrm{SK}(\exp W)$ with $\|W\|_\infty\le M$, for the exact projection or for any number of sweeps that ends with a row normalization. Then $\delta(H)\ge e^{-4M}/n$. For the exact projection, $\sigma_2(H)\le1-e^{-4M}$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Contraction

title: Proof
body_md: Write $H=n\delta\,(J/n)+(1-n\delta)R$ with $R\in\mathcal{B}_n$; this is a Doeblin splitting. On $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ the uniform part is zero, and $R$ is nonexpansive by (F1). This gives (a). Products act on $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ factor by factor, which gives (b). For (d), the column scalings have ratios at most $e^{2M}$. Thus two entries in one row differ by a factor of at most $e^{4M}$. Also, each row has an entry of at least $1/n$.

label: prop:rigidity
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:rigidity}
Let $\mathcal{C}_n:=\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}:\ A\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1},\ \|A\|_2\le1\}$ and $\mathcal{O}_1(n):=\{A\in\mathcal{C}_n:\ A^{\!\top} A=I\}$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=0pt,topsep=1pt,label=(\alph*)]
\item Every $A\in\mathcal{C}_n$ satisfies $A^{\!\top}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$, and $A$ is collapse-free if and only if $A\in\mathcal{O}_1(n)$. Also, $\mathcal{C}_n=\operatorname{conv}\mathcal{O}_1(n)$ and $\mathcal{B}_n=\mathcal{C}_n\cap\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}_{\ge0}$.
\item $\mathcal{B}_n\cap\mathcal{O}_1(n)=\mathfrak{S}_n$.
\item For $H\in\mathcal{B}_n$, $\sigma_2(H)=1$ if and only if $H$ is \emph{partly decomposable}. That is, there are sets $\mathcal R,\mathcal S\subset[n]$ with $0<|\mathcal R|=|\mathcal S|<n$ such that $H_{ij}=0$ if exactly one of $i\in\mathcal R$ and $j\in\mathcal S$ holds. In particular, $\sigma_2(H)<1$ for every $H\in\mathcal{B}_n^{\circ}$.
\item Let $H\in\mathcal{B}_n$ satisfy $\sigma_n(H)\ge1-\vartheta$ with $4n\vartheta<1$. Then $\varepsilon_\pi(H)\le4n\vartheta$ for some $\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_n$.
\end{enumerate}

If $W_k\in\mathcal{T}$ and $\Phi(W_k)\to P_\pi$, then $\|W_k\|_\infty\to\infty$.

body_md:
\label{rem:cost}
mHC backpropagates through the Sinkhorn loop with a dedicated kernel \citep[Sec.~4.3]{xie2026mhc}. By Theorem~\ref{thm:induced}(c), the straight-through update skips this backward pass, and it is not an approximation. It is exact entropic mirror descent, a natural-gradient method with its own convergence theory \citep{beck2003mirror}. Remark~\ref{rem:truncated-three-way} discusses the truncated projection.

label: rem:dynamic
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:dynamic}
In mHC the logits are $W=\lambda\,\mathrm{mat}(\tilde x\varphi)+b$. Here $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$, $\varphi$, and $b$ are trainable, and $\tilde x\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times nd}$ is a normalized vector that depends on the input. For one input, gradient flow on $b$ induces exactly $\dot W=-\nabla_W(f\circ\Phi)$. Gradient flow on $\varphi$ induces $\dot W=-\lambda^2\|\tilde x\|_2^2\,\nabla_W(f\circ\Phi)$, the same flow at a different speed. For a batch, the update averages the logit gradients of the inputs with the Gram weights $\lambda^2\langle \tilde x,\tilde x'\rangle$. Thus every statement about the logit flow holds input by input, up to this positive semidefinite weighting.

title: Proof
body_md: By the Cauchy--Binet formula and Cramer's rule, a weighted least-squares solution is a convex combination of the solutions of the square subsystems \citep{bental1990geometric}. For the additive model, the nonsingular square subsystems are the spanning trees of the complete bipartite graph $K_{n,n}$. On a tree, the fitted value of a cell is an alternating sum of data along a path with at most $2n-1$ edges. A Hamiltonian path with data $\pm1$ shows that the bound is sharp.

head: environment
name: Vertex viscosity of the logit flow

title: Proof
body_md: Along the flow, $\log H_{ij}=W_{ij}+\alpha_i+\beta_j$. The logit velocity $\dot W$ is the Fisher--Rao gradient, so it is $O(\varepsilon)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:small-grad}. If we differentiate the marginal constraints, we see that $\dot\alpha_i+\dot\beta_j$ is the weighted additive fit of $-\dot W$. Thus it is also $O(\varepsilon)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:additive}. The result is $|\dot\varepsilon|\le c\,\varepsilon^2$, which we integrate with Dini derivatives because $\varepsilon$ is only Lipschitz.

title: Proof
body_md: Along the flow, $H(t)$ is the scaling of $\exp(W_0)\odot(P_\pi+e^{-t}(J-P_\pi))$. Thus each entry off $\pi$ has a factor $e^{-t}$, and the scaling vectors could, in principle, cancel it. They cannot. A chain of entries off $\pi$, none of them small, closes into a cycle. The product of the entries of a cycle does not depend on the scaling, up to bounded factors.

label: cor:price
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:price}
Let $c_0\in(0,1)$. Assume that the residual path of an $L$-layer network preserves the difference channel up to the factor $c_0$, that is, $\sigma_n(H_{L:0})\ge c_0$. Let $\varepsilon_\star:=8n(n-1)\log(1/c_0)/L<1$. Then at least half of the layers satisfy $\varepsilon(H_l)\le\varepsilon_\star$. From a common start $\varepsilon_0>\varepsilon_\star$, the logit gradient flow needs time at least $(1/\varepsilon_\star-1/\varepsilon_0)/(4n^3G)$ to reach this configuration, which is linear in $L$. The corresponding lower bound for the Fisher--Rao flow, $\log(\varepsilon_0/\varepsilon_\star)/(2nG)$, grows only as $\log L$.

label: rem:adam
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:adam}
mHC trains with AdamW \citep{kingma2015adam}, which divides each update by a running root-mean-square of the gradient coordinate. Near a vertex the logit gradient is $O(\varepsilon)$ by \eqref{eq:flat}, but its running root-mean-square is also $O(\varepsilon)$. Thus the normalized update is $O(\eta)$, and Adam moves at an exponential rate (Figure~\ref{fig:main}(b,c)). Theorem~\ref{thm:viscosity} is therefore a statement about gradient flow, gradient descent, and the landscape. The landscape is flat at every vertex for every loss, so every optimizer receives a gradient signal of size $O(\varepsilon)$. The collapse of Section~\ref{sec:signal} and the budget limit of Section~\ref{sec:sinkhorn} do not depend on the optimizer.

body_md:
\label{prop:drift}
For $l<L$, let $H_l$ be nonnegative and row-stochastic, with column sums in $[1-e_l,1+e_l]$ and $e_l\le\frac12$. (Any number of sweeps that ends with a row normalization gives a nonnegative row-stochastic matrix.) Then $H_{L:l}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$, every column sum of $H_{L:l}$ is in $[e^{-2\sum_ie_i},e^{\sum_ie_i}]$, and $\|H_{L:l}\|_2\le e^{\frac12\sum_ie_i}$.

label: rem:budget
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:budget}
Let $r_0$ be the initial relative error of a layer, and let $\gamma$ be a target for the accumulated error $\sum_le_l$. Proposition~\ref{prop:knight} suggests that a layer with horizon $\tau_l$ needs about $\frac{\tau_l}{2}\log\frac{Lr_0}{\gamma}$ sweeps. Conversely, $t_{\max}$ sweeps give the accuracy $\gamma/L$ only to layers with $\tau_l\lesssim2t_{\max}/\log(Lr_0/\gamma)$. For mHC, $t_{\max}=20$, $L=60$, the observed drift $1.6=e^{0.47}$ gives $\gamma\approx0.47$, and $r_0\approx1$; thus the limit is $\tau\lesssim8$ layers. This is a heuristic scaling law, because Proposition~\ref{prop:knight} is asymptotic. Remark~\ref{rem:hilbert} gives a worst-case bound in Hilbert's projective metric.

label: prop:isometric
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:isometric}
Let $H_l\in\mathcal{O}_1(n)$ for all $l$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=0pt,topsep=1pt,label=(\alph*)]
\item The recursions \eqref{eq:two-channel} hold, and $H_{L:l}$ preserves the norm of every stream difference. Thus the horizon is infinite.
\item All singular values of the residual-path Jacobian are one, at every depth. This is dynamical isometry of the residual path \citep{pennington2017resurrecting}.
\item For $A\in\mathcal{O}_1(n)$, $T_A\mathcal{O}_1(n)=\{A\Omega:\ \Omega^{\!\top}=-\Omega,\ \Omega\mathbf{1}=0\}$. For the Frobenius metric, the Riemannian gradient of $f$ is $AQ\operatorname{skew}(A^{\!\top}\nabla f(A))Q$, with $\operatorname{skew}(X):=\frac12(X-X^{\!\top})$. The Cayley map $R_A(A\Omega):=A(I-\frac12\Omega)^{-1}(I+\frac12\Omega)$ is a retraction on $\mathcal{O}_1(n)$.
\end{enumerate}

label: rem:convex-relaxation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:convex-relaxation}
The set $\mathcal{C}_n=\operatorname{conv}\mathcal{O}_1(n)$ of mean-preserving nonexpansive mixers is convex (Proposition~\ref{prop:rigidity}(a)), and its Frobenius projection is explicit: $A\mapsto J/n+U\,\mathrm{clip}(U^{\!\top} AU)\,U^{\!\top}$. Here $\mathrm{clip}$ replaces every singular value larger than one by one. Thus projected gradient descent on $\mathcal{C}_n$ is available. But the interior of $\mathcal{C}_n$ consists of contractions, and they collapse exactly as the interior of $\mathcal{B}_n$ does. The difference is in the collapse-free part. For $\mathcal{C}_n$ it is the connected manifold $\mathcal{O}_1(n)$, on which Riemannian methods can move; for $\mathcal{B}_n$ it is the finite set $\mathfrak{S}_n$. The spectral-sphere design of \citet{liu2026shc} is a relaxation of the same kind for the full orthogonal group.

label: aux:cb
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{aux:cb}
Let $X,Y\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}$ with $m\ge p$, and let $D=\operatorname{diag}(\omega)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$. Then
\[
\det(X^{\!\top} DY)=\sum_{S\subseteq[m],\ |S|=p}\omega_S\,\det(X_S)\det(Y_S),\qquad \omega_S:=\prod_{s\in S}\omega_s ,
\]
where $X_S$ is the $p\times p$ submatrix of $X$ with the rows in $S$ \citep[Section~0.8.7]{horn2013matrix}. If $X\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ is nonsingular and $Xz=y$, then $z_r=\det(X^{(r)})/\det(X)$, where $X^{(r)}$ is $X$ with its $r$-th column replaced by $y$ (Cramer's rule).

label: aux:tree
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{aux:tree}
Let $(V,E)$ be a connected graph, and give its edges arbitrary orientations. Let $B\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|\times|E|}$ be the signed incidence matrix: $B_{ve}=+1$ if $v$ is the head of $e$, $B_{ve}=-1$ if $v$ is the tail of $e$, and $B_{ve}=0$ otherwise. Let $B_0$ be $B$ with one row removed. For a set $T\subseteq E$ of $|V|-1$ edges, the square submatrix of $B_0$ with the columns in $T$ is nonsingular if and only if $T$ is a spanning tree of the graph. In that case its determinant is $\pm1$ \citep[Chapter~2]{bapat2014graphs}.

label: aux:hilbert
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{aux:hilbert}
Let $K>0$, and let $\theta(K):=\max_{i,j,k,l}K_{ik}K_{jl}/(K_{jk}K_{il})$ and $\kappa(K):=(\sqrt{\theta(K)}-1)/(\sqrt{\theta(K)}+1)$. The map $x\mapsto Kx$ multiplies Hilbert's projective metric on the positive orthant by at most $\kappa(K)$ \citep{birkhoff1957extensions}. Thus the Sinkhorn scaling vectors converge linearly in this metric, with a factor of at most $\kappa(K)^2$ per sweep \citep{franklin1989scaling}, \citep[Theorems~4.1--4.2]{peyre2019computational}.

label: lem:gauge-complement
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:gauge-complement}
Let $H\in\mathcal{B}_n^{\circ}$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em,itemsep=1pt,label=(\alph*)]
\item The $g_H$-orthogonal complement of $\mathcal{T}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is $H\odot\mathfrak{s}$, and $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}=\mathcal{T}\oplus(H\odot\mathfrak{s})$.
\item For every $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, the affine space $\xi+H\odot\mathfrak{s}$ meets $\mathcal{T}$ in exactly one point, namely $\Pi_H(\xi)$. This point is given by \eqref{eq:FRproj}.
\item $\ker\Pi_H=H\odot\mathfrak{s}$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Gauge complement

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{steps}
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}1}.] A matrix $\xi$ is $g_H$-orthogonal to $\mathcal{T}$ if and only if $\xi\in H\odot\mathfrak{s}$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  By \eqref{eq:FR}, $g_H(\xi,\zeta)=\langle \xi\oslash H,\zeta\rangle$. Thus $\xi$ is $g_H$-orthogonal to $\mathcal{T}$ if and only if $\xi\oslash H\in\mathcal{T}^\perp=\mathfrak{s}$, that is, $\xi\in H\odot\mathfrak{s}$.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}2}.] $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}=\mathcal{T}\oplus(H\odot\mathfrak{s})$, and the sum is $g_H$-orthogonal.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  The map $s\mapsto H\odot s$ is injective because $H>0$. Thus $\dim(H\odot\mathfrak{s})=\dim\mathfrak{s}=2n-1$, and $\dim\mathcal{T}+\dim(H\odot\mathfrak{s})=(n-1)^2+2n-1=n^2$. By {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}1} the two subspaces are $g_H$-orthogonal, so they meet only in $0$.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}3}.] Let $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$. Then $\Pi_H(\xi)=\xi-H\odot(a\mathbf{1}^{\!\top}+\mathbf{1} b^{\!\top})$, where $(a,b)$ solves \eqref{eq:FRproj}.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  By {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}2}, $\xi=\Pi_H(\xi)+H\odot s$ for a unique $s=a\mathbf{1}^{\!\top}+\mathbf{1} b^{\!\top}\in\mathfrak{s}$. The condition $\Pi_H(\xi)\in\mathcal{T}$ says that the row sums and the column sums of $\xi-H\odot s$ are zero:
\[
\textstyle\sum_j\xi_{ij}-\sum_jH_{ij}(a_i+b_j)=0,\qquad \sum_i\xi_{ij}-\sum_iH_{ij}(a_i+b_j)=0 .
\]
The rows and the columns of $H$ sum to one, so these equations are \eqref{eq:FRproj}.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}4}.]{\sffamily\small\color{navy}Q.E.D.}
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  Steps {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}1} and {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}2} give (a). By {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}2}, the affine space $\xi+H\odot\mathfrak{s}$ meets $\mathcal{T}$ in exactly one point, and by {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}3} this point is $\Pi_H(\xi)$; this gives (b). By {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}2}, $\Pi_H(\xi)=0$ if and only if $\xi\in H\odot\mathfrak{s}$; this gives (c).
\end{steps}

label: lem:fit-normal
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:fit-normal}
Let $H\in\mathcal{B}_n^{\circ}$, $C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, and $(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n$. The following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.6em,itemsep=1pt,label=(\roman*)]
\item $a_i+\sum_jH_{ij}b_j=\sum_jH_{ij}C_{ij}$ for all $i$, and $b_j+\sum_iH_{ij}a_i=\sum_iH_{ij}C_{ij}$ for all $j$.
\item $(a,b)$ minimizes $F(a,b):=\sum_{i,j}H_{ij}\,(C_{ij}-a_i-b_j)^2$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently $\Pi_H(H\odot C)=H\odot(C-m)$, where $m=a\mathbf{1}^{\!\top}+\mathbf{1} b^{\!\top}$ is the weighted least-squares fit of $C$ by an additive model with weights $H$.
head: environment
name: Balancing equations are normal equations

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{steps}
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}1}.] The minimizers of $F$ are exactly its stationary points.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  $F$ is a convex quadratic function of $(a,b)$.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}2}.] The stationary points of $F$ are exactly the solutions of (i).
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  The partial derivatives of $F$ are zero if and only if
\[
\textstyle\sum_jH_{ij}(C_{ij}-a_i-b_j)=0\ \ (i\in[n]),\qquad
\sum_iH_{ij}(C_{ij}-a_i-b_j)=0\ \ (j\in[n]).
\]
Because $\sum_jH_{ij}=1=\sum_iH_{ij}$, these equations are the equations in (i).
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}3}.]{\sffamily\small\color{navy}Q.E.D.}
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  Steps {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}1} and {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}2} give the equivalence. The equations (i) are \eqref{eq:FRproj} with $\xi=H\odot C$. Thus Lemma~\ref{lem:gauge-complement}(b) gives $\Pi_H(H\odot C)=H\odot C-H\odot m$.
\end{steps}

label: lem:two-block
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:two-block}
Let $H\in\mathcal{B}_n$, and let $[\mathbf{1}/\sqrt n,\ U]$ be an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ($U^{\!\top} U=I$, $U^{\!\top}\mathbf{1}=0$). Then $H=J/n+QHQ$, the subspaces $\mathbb{R}\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ are invariant under $H$ and $H^{\!\top}$, and in this basis
\[
H=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&U^{\!\top} HU\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus the singular values of $H$ are $1$ and the singular values of $U^{\!\top} HU$. In particular $\sigma_2(H)=\|U^{\!\top} HU\|_2$ and $|\det(U^{\!\top} HU)|=\prod_{i=2}^n\sigma_i(H)$. The same statements hold for products of doubly stochastic matrices.

Let $H,H'\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}_{>0}$ and $0<\lambda\le\lambda'$ satisfy $\lambda H_{ij}\le H'_{ij}\le\lambda' H_{ij}$ for all $(i,j)$. Then $\lambda\,\varepsilon_\pi(H)\le\varepsilon_\pi(H')\le\lambda'\varepsilon_\pi(H)$ for every $\pi$, and $\lambda\,\varepsilon(H)\le\varepsilon(H')\le\lambda'\varepsilon(H)$.

body_md:
\label{lem:dini}
Let $\psi:[0,T)\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous, let $c\in\mathbb{R}$, and assume that
\[
D^+\psi(t):=\limsup_{h\downarrow0}\frac{\psi(t+h)-\psi(t)}{h}\ \le\ c\qquad\text{for every }t\in[0,T).
\]
Then $\psi(t)\le\psi(0)+ct$ for all $t\in[0,T)$.

x^{\perp}_L=H_{L:l}\,x^{\perp}_l+\sum_{i=l}^{L-1}H_{L:i+1}\,Q(h^{\mathrm{post}}_i)^{\!\top} u_i .

\begin{steps}
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}1}.] For every $H\in\mathcal{B}_n$, $\sigma_2(H)\le1-n\delta(H)$.
\begin{steps}
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}1}.] {\sffamily\small\color{navy}Let:}\  $\delta:=\delta(H)$. {\sffamily\small\color{navy}Case:}\  $n\delta=1$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  Every entry is at least $1/n$, and every row sums to one. Thus $H=J/n$, and $\sigma_2(H)=\|JQ\|_2/n=0=1-n\delta$.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}2}.] {\sffamily\small\color{navy}Case:}\  $n\delta<1$. {\sffamily\small\color{navy}Let:}\  $R:=(H-\delta J)/(1-n\delta)$. Then $R\in\mathcal{B}_n$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  $R\ge0$ because $H_{ij}\ge\delta$. Each row sum and each column sum of $R$ is $(1-n\delta)/(1-n\delta)=1$.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}3}.] {\sffamily\small\color{navy}Case:}\  $n\delta<1$. Then $\|Hx\|_2\le(1-n\delta)\|x\|_2$ for every $x\perp\mathbf{1}$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  For $x\perp\mathbf{1}$ we have $Jx=0$. Thus $Hx=(1-n\delta)Rx+\delta Jx=(1-n\delta)Rx$, and $\|R\|_2\le1$ by {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}2} and (F1).
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}4}.]{\sffamily\small\color{navy}Q.E.D.}
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  The two cases cover all $H$, because $n\delta\le1$. In the second case, {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}3} and $\sigma_2(H)=\|HQ\|_2$ give the claim.
\end{steps}
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}2}.] Equality holds for $H=(1-t)P_\pi+tJ/n$, $t\in[0,1]$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  The entries of $H$ off $\pi$ are $t/n$, and the entries on $\pi$ are $1-t+t/n\ge t/n$. Thus $\delta(H)=t/n$. For $x\perp\mathbf{1}$, $Hx=(1-t)P_\pi x$ and $\|P_\pi x\|_2=\|x\|_2$. Thus $\sigma_2(H)=1-t=1-n\delta(H)$.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}3}.] Part (b) holds.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  By (F3), each $H_i$ maps $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ into $\mathbf{1}^\perp$, and on $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ it has norm $\sigma_2(H_i)$. Thus $\|H_{L:l}x\|_2\le\prod_i\sigma_2(H_i)\|x\|_2$ for $x\perp\mathbf{1}$. Then {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}1} and $1-s\le e^{-s}$ give the second inequality.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}4}.] Part (c) holds.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  By (F2), $H_{L:l}\in\mathcal{B}_n$, so $H_{L:l}J=J$ and $H_{L:l}-J/n=H_{L:l}Q$. For unit vectors $e_j,e_k$,
\[
\big|(H_{L:l})_{jk}-\tfrac1n\big|=|e_j^{\!\top} H_{L:l}Qe_k|\le\|H_{L:l}Q\|_2=\sigma_2(H_{L:l}).
\]
The limit statement then follows from (b).
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}5}.] {\sffamily\small\color{navy}Assume:}\  $H=\mathrm{SK}(\exp W)$ with $\|W\|_\infty\le M$, for the exact projection or for a truncated iteration that ends with a row normalization. {\sffamily\small\color{navy}Prove:}\  $\delta(H)\ge e^{-4M}/n$.
\begin{steps}
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}1}.] {\sffamily\small\color{navy}Let:}\  $K:=\exp W$. Then $H=\operatorname{diag}(\mu)K\operatorname{diag}(\nu)$ with $\mu,\nu>0$, and $\nu_j=1/\sum_i\mu'_iK_{ij}$ for some $\mu'>0$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  For the exact projection, the column sums of $H$ are one, so this holds with $\mu'=\mu$. For a truncated iteration, the last column normalization sets $\nu$, and $\mu'$ is the row scaling at that moment.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}2}.] $\nu_j/\nu_k\ge e^{-2M}$ for all $j,k$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  Let $s:=\sum_i\mu'_i$. Because $K_{ij}\in[e^{-M},e^M]$, we have $\sum_i\mu'_iK_{ij}\in[e^{-M}s,e^{M}s]$, so $\nu_j\in[e^{-M}/s,e^{M}/s]$ by {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}1}.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}3}.] $H_{ij}/H_{ik}\ge e^{-4M}$ for all $i,j,k$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  $H_{ij}/H_{ik}=(K_{ij}/K_{ik})(\nu_j/\nu_k)\ge e^{-2M}e^{-2M}$ by {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}2}.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}4}.]{\sffamily\small\color{navy}Q.E.D.}
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  Row $i$ of $H$ sums to one, so $H_{ik}\ge1/n$ for some $k$. By {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}3}, $H_{ij}\ge e^{-4M}/n$ for every $j$.
\end{steps}
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}6}.] For the exact projection, $\sigma_2(H)\le1-e^{-4M}$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  For the exact projection $H\in\mathcal{B}_n$. Apply {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}1} and {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}5}.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}7}.]{\sffamily\small\color{navy}Q.E.D.}
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  Steps {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}1} and {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}2} give (a), {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}3} gives (b), {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}4} gives (c), and {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}5} and {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}6} give (d).
\end{steps}

\begin{steps}
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}1}.] Every $A\in\mathcal{C}_n$ satisfies $A^{\!\top}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$, and $A$ maps $\mathbf{1}^\perp$ into $\mathbf{1}^\perp$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality and $\|A^{\!\top}\|_2=\|A\|_2\le1$,
\[
n=\mathbf{1}^{\!\top} A\mathbf{1}=\langle A^{\!\top}\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1}\rangle\le\|A^{\!\top}\mathbf{1}\|_2\,\|\mathbf{1}\|_2\le\|\mathbf{1}\|_2^2=n .
\]
Thus both inequalities are equalities. Equality in the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, together with $\|A^{\!\top}\mathbf{1}\|_2=\|\mathbf{1}\|_2$, gives $A^{\!\top}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$. For $x\perp\mathbf{1}$, $\langle Ax,\mathbf{1}\rangle=\langle x,A^{\!\top}\mathbf{1}\rangle=0$.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}2}.] $\mathcal{C}_n=\{J/n+UBU^{\!\top}:\ B\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-1)\times(n-1)},\ \|B\|_2\le1\}$, where $U$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbf{1}^\perp$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  Let $A\in\mathcal{C}_n$. By {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}1}, $A$ preserves $\mathbb{R}\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{1}^\perp$, so $A=J/n+U(U^{\!\top} AU)U^{\!\top}$, and $\|U^{\!\top} AU\|_2\le\|A\|_2\le1$. Conversely, $J/n+UBU^{\!\top}$ fixes $\mathbf{1}$, and it is block diagonal in the basis $[\mathbf{1}/\sqrt n,\ U]$ with blocks $1$ and $B$. Thus its norm is at most one.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}3}.] For $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-1)\times(n-1)}$, the matrix $J/n+UZU^{\!\top}$ is in $\mathcal{O}_1(n)$ if and only if $Z\in O(n-1)$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  Because $U^{\!\top}\mathbf{1}=0$, we have $(J/n+UZU^{\!\top})^{\!\top}(J/n+UZU^{\!\top})=J/n+UZ^{\!\top} ZU^{\!\top}$. This matrix equals $I=J/n+UU^{\!\top}$ if and only if $Z^{\!\top} Z=I$.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}4}.] An element $A\in\mathcal{C}_n$ is collapse-free if and only if $A\in\mathcal{O}_1(n)$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  Write $A=J/n+UBU^{\!\top}$ as in {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}2}. For $x=Uy\perp\mathbf{1}$, $\|Ax\|_2=\|By\|_2$ and $\|x\|_2=\|y\|_2$. Thus $A$ is collapse-free if and only if $B$ is orthogonal, that is, by {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}3}, if and only if $A\in\mathcal{O}_1(n)$.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}5}.] $\mathcal{C}_n=\operatorname{conv}\mathcal{O}_1(n)$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  The set $\mathcal{C}_n$ is convex, and it contains $\mathcal{O}_1(n)$. Conversely, let $A=J/n+UBU^{\!\top}\in\mathcal{C}_n$. By Lemma~\ref{aux:convO}, $B=\sum_s\lambda_sZ_s$ with $Z_s\in O(n-1)$, $\lambda_s\ge0$, and $\sum_s\lambda_s=1$. Thus $A=\sum_s\lambda_s(J/n+UZ_sU^{\!\top})$, and each term is in $\mathcal{O}_1(n)$ by {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}3}.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}6}.] $\mathcal{B}_n=\mathcal{C}_n\cap\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}_{\ge0}$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  By (F1), $\mathcal{B}_n\subseteq\mathcal{C}_n$. Conversely, if $A\ge0$, $A\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$, and $\|A\|_2\le1$, then $A^{\!\top}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$ by {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}1}, so $A\in\mathcal{B}_n$.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}7}.] $\mathcal{B}_n\cap\mathcal{O}_1(n)=\mathfrak{S}_n$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  Let $A\in\mathcal{B}_n\cap\mathcal{O}_1(n)$. Then $\|A\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\!\top} A)=n$. Also $0\le A_{ij}\le1$, so $\sum_{ij}A_{ij}^2\le\sum_{ij}A_{ij}=n$, with equality if and only if every entry is $0$ or $1$. A doubly stochastic matrix with entries in $\{0,1\}$ is a permutation matrix. Conversely, permutation matrices are orthogonal and doubly stochastic.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}8}.] For $H\in\mathcal{B}_n$, $\sigma_2(H)=1$ if and only if $H$ is partly decomposable.
\begin{steps}
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}1}.] If $H$ is partly decomposable, then $\sigma_2(H)=1$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  Let $\mathcal R,\mathcal S$ be as in the definition, and let $k:=|\mathcal R|=|\mathcal S|$. Let $x:=\mathbf 1_{\mathcal S}/k-\mathbf 1_{\mathcal S^c}/(n-k)$, so $x\perp\mathbf{1}$. For $i\in\mathcal R$, row $i$ is supported in $\mathcal S$ and sums to one, so $(Hx)_i=1/k$. For $i\notin\mathcal R$, row $i$ is supported in $\mathcal S^c$, so $(Hx)_i=-1/(n-k)$. Thus
\[
\|Hx\|_2^2=\frac{k}{k^2}+\frac{n-k}{(n-k)^2}=\|x\|_2^2 ,
\]
so $\sigma_2(H)\ge1$, and $\sigma_2(H)\le1$ by (F1).
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}2}.] If $\sigma_2(H)=1$, then $H$ is partly decomposable.
\begin{steps}
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle3\rangle}1}.] There is $x\perp\mathbf{1}$, $x\ne0$, with $H^{\!\top} Hx=x$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  By compactness, there is a unit vector $x\perp\mathbf{1}$ with $\|Hx\|_2=1$. By (F1), $I-H^{\!\top} H$ is positive semidefinite, and $\langle (I-H^{\!\top} H)x,x\rangle=0$. Thus $(I-H^{\!\top} H)x=0$.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle3\rangle}2}.] The matrix $N:=H^{\!\top} H$ is reducible.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  $N$ is symmetric, nonnegative, and doubly stochastic, so its spectral radius is $1$, with eigenvector $\mathbf{1}$. By {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle3\rangle}1}, the eigenvalue $1$ is not simple. By Theorem~\ref{aux:pf}(a), $N$ is not irreducible.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle3\rangle}3}.] There is a nonempty proper subset $\mathcal S\subset[n]$ such that no row of $H$ has entries in both $\mathcal S$ and $\mathcal S^c$.
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  By {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle3\rangle}2} and Theorem~\ref{aux:pf}(b), there is a nonempty proper $\mathcal S$ with $N_{jk}=\sum_iH_{ij}H_{ik}=0$ for $j\in\mathcal S$ and $k\notin\mathcal S$. All terms are nonnegative, so $H_{ij}H_{ik}=0$ for every $i$.
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle3\rangle}4}.]{\sffamily\small\color{navy}Q.E.D.}
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  Each row of $H$ sums to one, so by {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle3\rangle}3} it is supported either in $\mathcal S$ or in $\mathcal S^c$. Let $\mathcal R$ be the set of rows supported in $\mathcal S$. If we sum the columns in $\mathcal S$, we get
\[
|\mathcal S|=\sum_{j\in\mathcal S}\sum_iH_{ij}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal R}\sum_{j\in\mathcal S}H_{ij}=|\mathcal R| .
\]
Thus $0<|\mathcal R|=|\mathcal S|<n$. By construction $H_{ij}=0$ if $i\in\mathcal R$ and $j\notin\mathcal S$, or if $i\notin\mathcal R$ and $j\in\mathcal S$.
\end{steps}
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}3}.]{\sffamily\small\color{navy}Q.E.D.}
\par{\sffamily\small\color{muted}Proof:}\  Steps {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}1} and {\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle2\rangle}2} give the equivalence. A positive matrix is not partly decomposable, so $\sigma_2<1$ on $\mathcal{B}_n^{\circ}$.
\end{steps}
\item[{\color{refcool}\ensuremath{\langle1\rangle}9}.] {\sffamily\small\color{navy}Assume:}\  $H\in\mathcal{B}_n$, $\sigma_n(H)\ge1-\vartheta$, and $4n\vartheta<1$. {\sffamily\small\color{navy}Prove:}\  $\varepsilon_\pi(H)\le4n\vartheta$ for some $\pi$.
